title: "Master!"
hook: Zuigan calls to himself each day, "Master!" and answers "Yes!" (Gateless Gate 12)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man up a tree, hanging by the teeth, with a question coming from below. Your line: hanging by the teeth. When a choice squeezed you, did you take a breath before grabbing for an exit? Day one thousand two hundred forty-three.

Somewhere in a monastery in old China, a monk calls out: Master! He isn't calling anyone else. He answers himself: Yes! Then he goes on. Wake up! Yes! From now on, don't be fooled by anyone. Yes! Yes! The Gateless Gate says he did this every day. A stranger walking past might wonder about him. Zen keeps the story as case twelve. Today, the monk who called his own name.

First, the man. His name is Ruiyan, Zuigan in Japanese. The case gives one picture of him: a daily habit of calling out to himself and answering. Master, in this story, isn't a teacher across the room. It's the one inside, the one the monk is trying to rouse. Second, the three calls. The first is just a name: are you there? The second is wake up: be here, not half asleep in your own life. The third is the longest: don't be fooled by others, any day, any time. That could mean other people's opinions. It could mean the stories the mind tells about itself. The case doesn't explain; it just lets him answer, yes, yes. Third, the twist. Wumen, the compiler, isn't simply impressed. In paraphrase, his comment says old Ruiyan buys and sells himself, putting on a whole set of masks: one to call, one to answer, one awake, one that won't be fooled. And then he warns that if you take any of those masks as the real thing, you've missed it. If you copy Ruiyan, Wumen says, your understanding is like a fox's. So the story isn't a tidy self-help trick. It's a daily practice that its own collector pokes at. Fourth, why it stays. For long stretches of a day, attention runs on its own, like a car with nobody checking the road. Calling your own name is one way to tap the shoulder. Some readers hear Ruiyan's practice as kind: he doesn't scold himself. He just calls, and answers yes. The question underneath stays open, and the koan leaves it there: who is it that answers?
screen: `RUIYAN CALLS HIS OWN NAME.` · `"MASTER!" "WAKE UP!" "DON'T BE FOOLED!"` · `WUMEN: SO MANY MASKS.` · `WHO IS IT THAT ANSWERS?` · then, large: `WAKE UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Sit and let the breath find its own pace. Silently, call your own name, the way a friend would from across a kitchen, warm and plain. Then answer, silently: yes. Notice what happens in the half second after the call. Is there a small waking up, a coming back to the room? Rest in that. When you drift, call again, just as kindly, and answer again. No scolding. Only the call and the yes. The bell holds the time.
Master! Ruiyan's daily call to himself in case twelve of the Gateless Gate, with his own answer, yes: wake up, and don't be fooled. Today's word.
Your line: wake up. Today, at one ordinary moment, a doorway or a red light, quietly call your own name and answer yes. See who shows up. Day one thousand two hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Zen students may be given this case as a koan; some also take Ruiyan's habit as a simple reminder, pausing during the day to call themselves back to attention.

fork.setup: you're Wumen, gathering this case into your collection. how do you comment on the monk who calls his own name each day?
options: praise it as the perfect method to copy.
tease him for wearing masks, and warn against imitation.

fork.reveal: Wumen says Ruiyan buys and sells himself with a set of masks, and that copying him gives a fox's understanding. even a practice worth keeping can turn into a role.

original.note: Chinese: the word Ruiyan calls out, often rendered 'master' or 'master of the house'. Pronunciation approximates Mandarin.

trapdoor: what you thought: a monk talking to himself.
what it means: a daily call to wake up, answered with a plain yes.
what a scholar hears: Gateless Gate case 12, where even Wumen's comment teases the masks, warning that copying Ruiyan misses the point.

notes: All of case 12 paraphrased (no public-domain English translation quoted). The spoken dialogue lines ('Master!' 'Yes!' 'Wake up!' 'Don't be fooled by anyone') are given as paraphrase in quotation-style speech; confirm they track the case: calls himself 'Master', answers 'Yes'; 'Be awake' / 'Yes'; 'Hereafter, don't be deceived by others' / 'Yes, yes.'

Wumen's comment paraphrased: Ruiyan buys and sells himself, wears many masks (one calling, one answering, one awake, one not deceived); recognizing any mask as real is wrong; imitating him is a fox's understanding. Confirm.
Original 主人公 ('master', lit. sometimes 'master of the house'): confirm the term used in the case and the gloss.
Setting 'in old China' is general; no date given. The car image and 'some readers hear the practice as kind' are interpretation.
